o: We build the final string by processing words in order; at each step the current accumulated string may be placed before or after the next word, saving one character whenever the touching boundary characters match. Only three things about the accumulated string matter for the future: its length, its first character, and its last character — interior content never affects later joins. So we run a DP whose state is (first char, last char) mapped to the minimum achievable length. There are at most 26×26 states and 1000 words, giving ~676k transitions. Example 1: words ["aa","ab","bc"] ends with state (a,c) of length 4. Example 3 shows why greedily appending fails — sometimes prepending wins.
k: Only (length, first char, last char) of the accumulated string matters; collapse all histories with the same (first, last) to the minimum length.
Each step tries both orders: join(acc, w) saves 1 if acc's last char equals w's first; join(w, acc) saves 1 if w's last char equals acc's first.

a.n: Approach 1: DP over (First Char, Last Char)
a.i: dp[(f, l)] = minimum length of any string obtainable so far starting with f and ending with l. Transition for word w (first fw, last lw, length wl): from state (f, l) with length L, appending gives state (f, lw) with length L + wl − (l == fw ? 1 : 0); prepending gives state (fw, l) with length L + wl − (lw == f ? 1 : 0). Answer is the minimum dp value after all words.
s: For each subsequent word, build a new dp by applying both join directions from every existing state.
a.t: O(n · 26²) — each word relaxes at most 676 states

a.i: At each step pick whichever join order yields the shorter intermediate string, tracking only the current string's endpoints. This is not always optimal globally (Example 3 defeats it) but serves as an intuitive starting point and a debugging reference.
s: Keep current first char, last char, length.
For each word, compare savings of appending vs prepending and take the better.

w: Present the DP; note the greedy fails on Example 3 ("aaa","c","aba") because sacrificing an immediate merge enables a bigger one later. Pitfalls: single-word input (answer = its length), and remembering both joins save at most one character each. Follow-up: what if words could be reordered arbitrarily? Then the state would need more bookkeeping.
